context: Current closing price of Aon (AON): $330.16 USD as of 2026-11-03.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift assumption from what appears to be a baseline price around 330–332. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the current level with only a slight upward nudge, reflecting the typical mean-reverting behavior of most financial assets over very short windows and the assumption that no major catalysts were immediately pending. For the one-week estimate, I projected a marginal continuation of that drift, acknowledging that short-term momentum, if present, tends to persist mildly but that mean reversion also applies. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 335 reflects a similarly modest trend assumption, essentially extrapolating a slow grind higher while recognizing that one month is long enough for meaningful fundamental or macro developments to materialize.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect increasing uncertainty as the time horizon extends, which is standard for any forward-looking price forecast. At one day, the range of roughly 17 points reflects normal daily volatility in what I assumed to be a moderately volatile instrument. By one week, the interval widens to 32 points, capturing the compounding of daily fluctuations and the possibility of a news-driven move. At one month, the interval stretches to 60 points, acknowledging that macro data releases, central bank communications, earnings surprises, or geopolitical events could all meaningfully shift the trajectory over that window.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include tail events such as a major surprise in central bank policy, an unexpected geopolitical escalation, a significant earnings miss or beat if this is an equity, or a sharp liquidity event in broader markets. On the upside, a risk-on sentiment surge or strong economic data could drive the price above 365 within a month. On the downside, a financial shock or sector-specific bad news could easily breach the lower bound of 305. These are not my base cases, but they are plausible scenarios that the 90% confidence interval explicitly leaves room for — roughly a 10% combined probability of landing outside those bounds.

It is also worth noting that without knowing the specific asset, the forecast carries additional model uncertainty because the appropriate volatility assumption and drift rate differ substantially across asset classes. If this is a fixed-income instrument, equity index, commodity, or individual stock, each would warrant different calibration of both the point estimate trajectory and the interval widths. That structural ambiguity is itself a source of unquantified uncertainty layered on top of the stated intervals.
